title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt-5-mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer, N=400 paired tasks (800 episodes) and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task delivered to both conditions). Confirmatory, artifact‑backed outcomes: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, 10,000 resamples); Cohen's h = 0.0. We emphasize that two preregistered design choices—shared_initial_generation semantics and reuse of the same deterministic validator as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer—produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for assessing generator×guard closed‑loop dynamics. We present the artifact‑backed execution and analysis, diagnose why the design produced a null outcome, and give concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for benchmark hardening to expose generator×guard interactions in future runs.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are advancing intent‑driven NetOps by producing device configuration artifacts and procedural change sequences (canaries, staged rollouts, rollback semantics). Prior work reports promise but also highlights crucial evaluation gaps: operational safety requires end‑to‑end tests that include generation, deterministic verification, staged rollout semantics, rollback, and provenance. To probe verifier utility under controlled conditions we preregistered a paired confirmatory study (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) comparing a verifier‑augmented pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1.

Research question. Under the preregistered action‑aware staging benchmark, does adding a deterministic runtime validator to an LLM pipeline increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in safe‑deploy rate (guarded − baseline) and the design was frozen prior to execution.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired evaluation using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5, with complete execution and analysis artifacts archived; (2) a transparent diagnosis of why preregistered design choices produced a deterministic ceiling effect in this run and how that invalidates the original power rationale for the primary estimand; (3) concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations to harden action‑aware benchmarks to expose generator×guard dynamics; (4) compact, artifact‑grounded execution and statistical summaries that enable reproducible follow‑on experiments.
sections.related_work: Intent translation and intent→configuration pipelines have been demonstrated in prototypes and benchmarks (intent‑based configuration, PreConfig, GraphSynth) where LLMs synthesize configuration artifacts from operator intent. Research in IaC shows verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair loops improve correctness in infrastructure provisioning contexts (e.g., TerraFormer), and deterministic verification and reachability tools detect configuration errors in offline and some online settings. Agentic and tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, multi‑agent orchestrations, RAG) are actively applied to AIOps and NetOps but introduce new failure modes—hallucination, misapplied tools, and calibration failures—that motivate runtime guardrails and staged deployment. Surveys and position papers emphasize a gap: standardized, action‑aware benchmarks that include staged rollout, blocking, repair, rollback, and provenance are limited; our study operationalizes a compact staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to probe verifier utility. The cited corpus (intent→config studies; verifier and IaC tool papers; calibration/self‑verification literature) motivates our paired design, the use of deterministic validators, and the recommendations we derive from the observed outcome.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand. We preregistered study cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1. The design prespecified a paired binary outcome across exactly N=400 tasks with paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline as the primary estimand. The confirmatory test was a permutation‑based paired difference (two‑sided, α=0.05) implemented per the preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor; an exact McNemar two‑sided check was included as corroboration. Bootstrap resampling parameters (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) were frozen for secondary bootstrap CIs.

Adapter semantics and generation policy. Execution used adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1 with declared generator gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json) and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as runtime guard and as the post‑hoc scorer. Key preregistered semantics: shared_initial_generation = true (independent_condition_generation = false), meaning the adapter requested one deterministic LLM generation per task that both the baseline and guarded episodes received. This semantic isolates validator acceptance behavior on identical generator outputs rather than exposing generator variance between conditions. The preregistration explicitly documented this choice and its intended interpretive scope.

Episode and model‑call accounting. The design planned 800 episodes (two episodes per task) and allowed up to one repair call per task. Under shared_initial_generation semantics each task used one LLM generation shared between conditions; model_calls_used = 400 while completed_episode_count = 800. Deterministic three‑replay consistency checks were preregistered: each agent+simulator pair was replayed three times and any non‑identical replays would flag a task for automated exclusion per the missingness_plan. The preregistration defined exclusion and missingness handling as automated and deterministic with no human adjudication.

Validator, scoring, and repair policy. The runtime validator applied full intent‑constraint validation (scorer_id deterministic_netops_validator_v5); by design the same validator implementation was used both to block/accept candidates at runtime and to score outcomes post‑hoc. The adapter permitted one repair attempt per task but repairs would only be invoked if the runtime guard policy triggered them. Repair traces and repair_applied flags were recorded in validator_trace fields for every episode.

Statistical analysis and reproducibility. Primary analysis used the preregistered permutation test on paired binary outcomes and reported exact permutation p‑values and Cohen's h for effect size. Secondary analysis comprised bootstrap percentile CIs for the paired difference (resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729) and descriptive diagnostics (failure‑mode cluster analysis where applicable). All analysis code, seeds, and artifacts (analysis/*) are archived. Deterministic reconciliation and provider‑call audits were performed and are recorded in analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json.

sections.discussion:
Construct‑validity diagnosis. The observed deterministic ceiling outcome directly results from two preregistered design choices: (1) shared_initial_generation semantics delivered identical generator outputs to baseline and guarded episodes, and (2) the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer are the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). When the validator deterministically accepted the shared candidate for every task, both conditions necessarily produced identical acceptances and post‑hoc scores, yielding n_11 = 400 and zero discordant pairs. Under these semantics the study measured validator acceptance on identical candidates rather than independent closed‑loop generator+guard dynamics; consequently the primary estimand is uninformative in this run.

Statistical and power implications. The preregistered power rationale assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates and intra‑pair variability; the observed ceiling invalidates those assumptions and collapses uncertainty estimates (bootstrapped CI = [0.0, 0.0]). The permutation and McNemar tests correctly reflect the observed identical outcomes (p = 1.0). Because outcomes were unanimous and deterministic, the confirmatory framework returned a degenerate but artifact‑consistent null observation.

Operational implications and benchmark hardening recommendations. The archived artifacts permit concrete, implementable recommendations to expose generator×guard dynamics in future runs without inventing new datasets: (A) set independent_condition_generation = true so each condition receives an independently sampled generator output and the runtime guard can block or allow divergent outcomes; (B) use heterogeneous implementations for runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer (avoid scorer/guard conflation) so acceptance and scoring are independent; (C) inject controlled adversarial/perturbation seeds over a prescribed fraction of tasks to guarantee non‑trivial baseline failure rates for power calculations; (D) enable and record repair invocations and repair outcomes in adapter traces to create measurable divergence in rollback/repair statistics; (E) adopt difficulty‑stratified sampling or oversample “very_hard” patterns to ensure the benchmark contains a measurable error rate that the confirmatory design can detect.

Threats to validity and generalizability. Model and scope: the run used a single declared generator (gpt‑5‑mini) and a single deterministic validator; results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity. Environment realism: the benchmark is synthetic and the simulator/validator do not capture all production telemetry noise or adversarial behaviors. Construct validity: reusing deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer conflates acceptance and scoring. Adversarial robustness and human‑in‑the‑loop efficacy remain untested in this run and require targeted designs.

Reproducibility and artifact availability. All runtime calls, raw LLM responses, validator traces, deterministic three‑replay checks, per‑task manifests, and analysis artifacts are archived in the artifact bundle (execution/* and analysis/*). Key artifacts referenced here: execution/execution_manifest.json (execution summary and model_calls_used), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (paired outcomes), analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg (bootstrap distribution), analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (analysis parameters), and execution/task_manifest.jsonl (full per‑task difficulty labels). Readers can reproduce the exact confirmatory analysis by running paired_binary_analysis_v1 over execution/raw_results.jsonl with the frozen seeds documented in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. Deterministic reconciliation verified completed pairs = 400 and that all deterministic consistency checks passed (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json).
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline and an LLM‑only pipeline on an action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the specific generator+validator pairing used, every shared candidate satisfied the deterministic runtime validator so both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy across N=400 pairs (paired difference = 0.0; permutation p = 1.0). This deterministic ceiling outcome is an artifact of preregistered design choices that removed opportunities for the runtime guard to alter outcomes; it does not imply that runtime verification lacks utility in heterogeneous, adversarial, or independently generated settings. We archive the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts so researchers can reproduce the run and use these artifacts as seeds for hardened experiments that exercise blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors under independent generation and adversarial perturbations.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.

Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open for future work.

Aggregated difficulty reporting gap: the full per‑task difficulty labels for all N=400 are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl but an aggregated histogram by difficulty level for the full sample was not included in the primary artifacts provided in-text; readers can derive the complete aggregation from execution/task_manifest.jsonl in the archived bundle. Representative sample difficulty counts (n=6) are included in the Results section to illustrate benchmark diversity.
